cse-2006-cs-65.approach: Split each job into I/O–CPU–I/O phases, schedule the CPU bursts by shortest remaining compute time (non-preemptively at the given decision points), and count the time the CPU has nothing ready.

steps.title: Start
steps.body: All start with I/O; the CPU is idle during 0–2. P1 becomes ready at 2 and computes 2–9 (P2 ready at 4, P3 at 6).

steps.title: Remaining bursts
steps.body: At 9, P1 goes to its final I/O (9–10). Shortest remaining compute is P2 (14): runs 9–23. Then P3 (21): runs 23–44.

steps.title: End
steps.body: P3 does its last I/O 44–47; nothing else is left, so the CPU is idle 44–47. Everything finishes at 47.

steps.title: Idle percentage
steps.body: Idle $= 2 + 3 = 5$ units of $47$: $\dfrac{5}{47} \times 100 \approx 10.6\%$.

optionAnalysis.reason: The CPU is idle at least during the first 2 units, when every process is in I/O.
5 idle units out of 47 → 10.6%.
30% does not match any idle interval in the schedule.
89.4% is the CPU utilisation (42/47), not idle time.

cse-2006-cs-66.approach: Only p and q can run now (they request nothing). When they finish, they free $x_p + x_q$ instances, and some other process $k$ must be able to proceed with them. Compare that requirement with each option.

steps.title: Free resources after p, q
steps.body: All instances are in use, so free $= 0$ now. p and q complete and release $x_p + x_q$ instances.

steps.title: Progress condition
steps.body: The system avoids deadlock only if at least one other process can then be satisfied: $x_p + x_q \ge y_k$ for some $k \ne p, q$, i.e. $x_p + x_q \ge \min_{k \ne p,q} y_k$ (the standard form of this question). The scan prints $\max$; with $\max$ the inequality guarantees that **every** other process can be satisfied right away. Either way, (B) is the only option relating the released resources $x_p + x_q$ to the outstanding requests $y_k$.

steps.title: Other options
steps.body: Options C and D constrain only the sizes of $x_p, x_q$ against 1, saying nothing about others' requests; option A ($\min(x_p,x_q) < \max y_k$) points the wrong way — it describes shortage, not safety.

optionAnalysis.reason: This says the smaller holding is below the largest request — a shortage condition, which does not prevent deadlock.
Compares the resources freed by p and q with the other processes' requests — the right form (min in the standard statement).
Holding more than one instance says nothing about whether released resources meet any request.
Same flaw as C: unrelated to the other processes' requests.

pitfalls: With $\max$ the condition is sufficient rather than necessary; the original question uses $\min$ — answer B in both readings.
cse-2006-cs-66.verification: Example: x_p = x_q = 1, y_k ∈ {3, 5}: released 2 < 3 → nobody can proceed (deadlock), and B fails as expected.
